h1: Stepping back from daily operations as a brewery founder
title: Stepping Back as a Brewery Founder | Craft Beer School
desc: How a brewery founder steps back from the floor: run an absence test, write the routines down, set authority limits and read the business through numbers.
teaser: Stepping back is not a holiday. It is a set of systems that let the brewery run on a Tuesday when you are not there.
standfirst: Most founders who try to step back end up pulled straight onto the floor again. The ones who manage it build the routines, the limits and the reports first, then leave in stages.
sections: Stepping back is a systems job

Founders usually decide to step back after a bad stretch: a missed family wedding, a health scare or a year without a day off. The instinct is to hand everything to the head brewer and walk away. That rarely lasts a month. Something breaks, the phone rings and the founder is back on the floor.

The founders who manage it treat stepping back as a project with stages. Write down what you do. Hand over each piece with a clear owner. Set limits on money and authority. Then replace your daily presence with a weekly and monthly view of the numbers. The goal is to stop being the only person who can run the brewery, while still caring how it runs.
Run a two week absence test

Before you plan anything, find out what actually depends on you. Take two weeks away, reachable only for genuine emergencies. Ask your team to log every question they would normally have brought to you.

The log is the plan. A typical list mixes the trivial with the serious: where the spare keg couplers are, whether to accept a malt delivery that arrived with damp bags, who signs the duty payment and what to do when the glycol chiller alarms at 2 am. Each item is either a missing document, a missing decision right or a missing skill. Sort them into those three piles and you know where to start.
Write the routines that replace you

Most of a brewery runs on routines the founder carries in their head. Put them on paper, one page each, kept where the work happens:

  • Brew sheets with targets and tolerances for every beer: mash temperature, original gravity, fermentation temperature and the gravity at which to raise temperature for a diacetyl rest.
  • Cleaning routines, for example a hot caustic clean typically at 1.5 to 2% strength and 70 to 80 °C, followed by a rinse and an acid step.
  • Opening and closing checklists for the taproom and cellar.
  • Who to call when the chiller, the boiler or the CO2 supply fails.
  • The excise register and the daily and monthly filings, with the dates.

Then test each document by asking someone else to follow it while you watch and say nothing.
Read the business through numbers, not the floor

When you are on the floor every day, you see problems with your own eyes. Once you step back, you need numbers to see them for you. Agree a weekly sheet of six to eight figures: litres brewed, litres sold, beer loss, food cost, staff cost, cash in the bank and any open safety or quality issues.

Each month, read the full profit and loss statement and the balance sheet, not only the bank balance. Our guides to reading a brewery profit and loss statement and reading a balance sheet walk through what each line means. A founder who reads these well can spot a creeping problem in creditors, stock or margin weeks before it shows up on the floor.

Stepping back without limits is how founders get nasty surprises. Decide in writing who can spend what. For example: the head brewer may order ingredients and spares up to ₹25,000 per order. The taproom manager may approve staff overtime within the monthly budget. Anything larger needs your approval or a second signature.

Set the bank up the same way. A second authorised signatory with a limit keeps salaries and duty payments flowing when you are away. A dual signature above that limit keeps control where it belongs. Review the limits every six months. Raise them when people prove themselves, which is a cheap way to say thank you.

Stepping back is easier when you know what you are stepping into. Most founders keep the brand and the final say on new beers. They also keep the relationships with landlords, banks and key accounts, plus decisions on new investment. Write your new role down in the same format as everyone else's.

If you have partners, check what your agreement says about a partner who is no longer working full time. Clauses on salaries, drawings and voting rights often assume everyone will stay on the floor. Our guide to brewery partner agreements covers the clauses to revisit with your lawyer.
Leave in stages and measure each one

Go from five days on the floor to three, then two, then one review day a week. Hold each stage for a full month and check the weekly numbers before taking the next. If beer loss or food cost moves the wrong way, fix the system that slipped rather than walking back in for good.

Knowing which numbers tell you the truth about a brewery you no longer see every day is a skill you can learn. Your first step: pick the dates for a two week absence in the next quarter and tell the team today, so they have time to start their question log.
faqs: How do I know what in my brewery depends on me?
Take two weeks away and have the team log every question they would normally bring to you. That log shows the missing documents, decision rights and skills.
What numbers should a founder watch after stepping back?
A weekly sheet of litres brewed and sold, beer loss, food cost, staff cost, cash and open issues, plus the full monthly profit and loss statement and balance sheet.
Does stepping back affect a partner agreement?
It can. Salaries, drawings and voting rights are often written assuming every partner works full time. Review the agreement with your lawyer before you change your role.
